lesson.title: Weaving Variables Straight into Text with f-strings
lesson.summary: An f-string is a string literal prefixed with the letter f that lets you embed variables and expressions directly inside curly braces, and Python evaluates and inserts each one automatically when the string is built.
lesson.body:
An f-string looks like a normal string except for one small change: an f placed immediately before the opening quote. That single letter tells Python to scan the string for anything wrapped in curly braces and treat it as live code to evaluate, rather than plain text. If name holds "Maria" and age holds 16, then print(f"{name} is {age} years old.") produces the output Maria is 16 years old. Python replaces {name} with the current value of the variable name and {age} with the current value of age, converting each to text automatically as it builds the final string.

What goes inside the curly braces does not have to be a bare variable name; it can be any expression. f"{2 + 3}" evaluates the arithmetic first and embeds the result, producing the string "5". A more realistic example uses a format specifier after a colon to control how a number displays: f"{price * 1.08:.2f}" first computes price * 1.08 following ordinary operator precedence, then formats that result to exactly two decimal places. If price is 19.995, the result is the string "21.59".

F-strings solve a real annoyance that string concatenation creates. Building the same greeting with + would require "Hello, " + name + "! You are " + str(age) + " years old.", with an explicit str() conversion needed anywhere a number appears, since + refuses to mix strings and numbers as covered in String Concatenation. The f-string version, f"Hello, {name}! You are {age} years old.", handles the conversion automatically and reads much closer to the sentence it produces, especially once more than one or two variables are involved.

F-strings depend directly on variables already existing, tying them to Variable Assignment: a name has to be bound to a value with = before an f-string can read it. It is worth being precise about timing here. An f-string captures the value of a variable at the exact moment the string is built, not a live link to the variable. If age changes to 17 later in the program, a greeting string already created still shows 16, because that string, like all strings, is immutable once it exists; only building a fresh f-string after the change would show the new value.

Beyond basic substitution, format specifiers offer finer control: :.2f rounds a float to two decimal places, and :, inserts thousands separators into large numbers. Those details go further than a first introduction needs, but the core pattern, f"literal text {variable} more text", is the tool worth mastering first, since it is by far the most common way modern Python code builds output that mixes fixed text with changing data.

An f-string can also hold several variables and pieces of literal text in any arrangement: f"{first} {last} scored {points} points" reads almost exactly like the sentence it produces, filling in first, last, and points wherever their curly braces appear. This readability advantage tends to grow, not shrink, as the number of variables in a message increases, which is why f-strings have largely replaced building longer messages out of many chained + operators in modern Python code.
